items.title: A reaction that gets cold all by itself
items.claim: Mix solid barium hydroxide octahydrate with solid ammonium thiocyanate in a beaker. The mixture turns into a slush and drops to about minus 20 degrees Celsius — cold enough to freeze the beaker to a wet wooden block.
items.prompt: How can a reaction proceed if it absorbs heat from its surroundings?

options.text: It can't — the textbook is wrong
Endothermic reactions only happen when energy is supplied externally
The enormous increase in entropy (two solids becoming liquid and gas) outweighs the unfavourable enthalpy change in the Gibbs equation
The reaction is actually exothermic at the molecular level — the cooling is an illusion

items.reveal_title: Entropy can drive a reaction uphill in enthalpy
items.reveal:
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. The reaction is strongly endothermic (positive delta H), but it produces 10 moles of liquid water plus 2 moles of ammonia gas from 2 moles of crystalline solid. The entropy change is huge and positive.

At room temperature T delta S is larger than delta H, so delta G is negative — the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds, sucking heat from the surroundings as it does.
items.why: Students learn 'exothermic equals spontaneous' as a rule of thumb. Entropy can outvote enthalpy when disorder rises sharply.

items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Carbon monoxide's dipole points the wrong way
items.claim: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon (3.44 versus 2.55). You would expect carbon monoxide to have a dipole with the negative end on oxygen. In fact the negative end sits on carbon.
items.prompt: Why does CO's dipole point from O (positive) to C (negative)?

options.text: Electronegativity values are wrong for small molecules
Oxygen donates a lone pair into a bonding orbital concentrated on carbon — the dative pi back-bonding cancels and reverses the simple electronegativity dipole
Carbon monoxide has no dipole at all
The molecule rotates so fast the dipole averages to zero

items.reveal_title: Molecular orbital theory beats Pauling's electronegativity table
items.reveal:
Drawing CO with a triple bond shows it as :C≡O: with a lone pair on each atom. But molecular orbital calculations and experiment agree: the highest occupied molecular orbital is the sigma orbital pointing AWAY from oxygen on the carbon side, giving carbon partial negative character.

This is exactly why CO is such a good ligand for transition metals — it bonds to metals through the carbon, donating that lone pair while accepting back-donation into empty pi-star orbitals. The whole of transition-metal carbonyl chemistry depends on it.
items.why: Electronegativity gives a crude bond-polarity estimate. For molecules with multiple bonds and lone pairs, the orbital picture matters more.
